newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Europe's finances to get lift from black economy.
newsitem.headline: Europe's finances to get lift from black economy.

text.p: Europe's public finance woes are set to lessen under plans to restate national accounts of all 15 European Union member states to include the size of their black economies.

However, European statisticians leading the drive to uncover the hidden wealth in the continent said the planned changes would probably come too late to have any impact calculation of 1997 deficits for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Friedrich Schneider, a professor at Linz university, Austria, estimated in a recent study that the black economies in many EU states exceeded 15 percent of their official wealth as measured by gross domestic product (GDP).
If EU states were to revise up their GDP levels by such a factor it would eradicate the budgetary problems at present associated with the EMU project.
When Italy carried out a similar exercise on its economy in 1987 its GDP went up overnight by 18 percent.
Unfortunately for the politicians, statisticians are adamant this will not happen at European level until after the selection of countries for EMU is made in late April or early May 1998.
The revisions, due to be notified to the European Commission by October 1998 at the latest, will also probably not be made public until April 1999.

"From 1998 there will probably be an impact on GDP change but the selection of candidates for EMU will be based on 1997 figures," one EU official said. "There has been an explicit request not to correct 1997 (GDP data)."

One official said in any case the changes he anticipated were nothing like as high as indicated in the Austrian study, noting most EU member states already adjusted national accounts by a margin representing the grey economy.
The EU project -- which dates back to 1994 -- was merely designed to harmonise the methodologies used, he added.
It was "theoretically possible" some countries might even have to revise down their GDP.

Belgium, which the Austrian study estimated has a black economy that exceeds 20 percent of GDP, already adjusts its accounts for hidden wealth, a Belgian official said. It was too early to say what impact the EU work would have, he said.
One official said other EU countries had also already had big revisions in their GDP since the early 1990s, partly to take account of hidden wealth.

The GDPs of Greece, Portugal, Luxembourg and Ireland had already been revised up by respectively 20 percent, 14 percent, 11 percent and five percent, according to a report presented to EU member states last year, he said.

"It would be extremely difficult to let these countries correct again by something like 20 percent," he said, noting GDP had to be revised by more than five percent before it had an impact on a country's deficit to GDP ratio.

Once revisions were made, they could also prove a double-edged sword for EU countries striving to keep public borrowing down as required for EMU and under the post-EMU stability pact, one official noted.
Because EU member states' contributions to the EU budget are partly based on the size of their GDP, countries which face large revisions will also face large requests for new transfers to the EU.
Countries which have struggled to meet the Maastricht Treaty criteria for 1997, could -- once in EMU -- have their budgets pushed up by new demands for funds from Brussels.
In addition, any new bills are to be backdated to 1988, the year the Commission first questioned countries' national accounts and requested they were re-examined on a common basis.
